title: A Winter for the Cellar
premise: Folklorist Ulyana Sterling arrives in the snowbound village of Vinterhollow to record its winter songs, only to learn each one is sung exactly once a year — because singing them twice wakes what the founders buried beneath the church. When an excavation crew breaches a cellar door sealed from the inside, the thing below begins borrowing voices, memories, and finally faces, and Ulyana discovers her own family name in the founders' ledger. To survive the deepening frost, she must complete the interrupted binding ritual with the help of Tomas, the gravedigger's son who loves her and whose duty demands she leave. In the end she sings the songs a second time herself, trading her recorded archive — and much of her own memory of him — to reseal the door, walking out of Vinterhollow belonging to the winter rather than to anyone.
about_author: Ansel Iversen is the pen name of a former archivist who spent six winters cataloguing oral histories in remote northern settlements before turning to fiction. They write horror about the tenderness required to remember things that would rather be forgotten.

chapters.title: The Songs Are Sung Once
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She arrives in Vinterhollow by mail sledge, recorder in hand, charmed by the village but unsettled when an old woman refuses to repeat a lullaby even for payment. The emotional beat is warm curiosity shadowed by first unease: everyone here is generous except about repetition.

chapters.title: Ledger of Founders
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Researching in the church vestry, she finds a founders' ledger listing a 'cellar rite' with her own surname among the signatories — impossible, she thinks, a coincidence. Beat: intellectual thrill curdling into personal dread as the parish priest, Father Aldous, quietly asks her to stop looking.

chapters.title: What the Crew Struck
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The road crew blasting a new culvert breaks into a stone door sealed from the inside, its hinges fused by frost from within. Tomas, who dug graves beside his father for twenty years, feels the ground go wrong under his boots. Beat: dread of something opened that was locked on purpose.

chapters.title: First Frost Pattern
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. That night frost climbs her window in patterns matching the ledger's marginal sigils, and she records a humming through the wall that no villager will acknowledge. Beat: isolation deepening; documentation begins to feel less like scholarship and more like prayer, as the blurb promises.

chapters.title: Tomas
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Ulyana and Tomas meet over tea at the inn; he warns her without explaining, and she finds in him the first person who doesn't flinch from her questions. Beat: tender connection kindling against a backdrop of communal silence — love beginning where belonging is withheld.

chapters.title: The Borrowed Voice
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Playing back her field recordings, she hears the old woman's lullaby sung twice — by a voice that isn't hers or the woman's. Villagers begin avoiding her street. Beat: horror arriving through her own instruments; the archive itself compromised.

chapters.title: Duty of the Gravedigger
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. His dying father confesses the family obligation: every generation, a Sterling must be kept ignorant until the door opens, then driven out before the frost takes them. Tomas must choose between the duty and the woman. Beat: love against duty made explicit and painful.

chapters.title: Faces in the Congregation
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. At Sunday service she counts the congregation and finds one extra face — a man wearing the features of a founder from a portrait downstairs. No one else reacts. Beat: uncanny escalation; the village's polite denial becomes complicity.

chapters.title: The Excavation Below
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Sent to inspect the breach, he descends and finds the tunnel lined with scratched tally marks — thousands of winters counted from the inside. Something down there has been patient, and counting. Beat: vertiginous dread; the scale of the thing revealed.

chapters.title: Memory of Salt
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She dreams memories that aren't hers: a cellar, a chain, a woman singing the binding song alone because the others fled. She wakes with salt-crusted lips and the melody complete in her head. Beat: inherited memory surfacing; she realizes the ritual lives in her bloodline.

chapters.title: Father Aldous Confesses
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. The priest admits the founders botched the original rite — they sealed the door from outside while the thing sealed it from within, leaving both sides half-bound. Each year's single singing maintains the fragile truce. Beat: exposition as confession; hope and despair entwined.

chapters.title: Leave Before the Frost Writes
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Tomas begs Ulyana to take the last mail sledge out, lying that he feels nothing for her. She sees through it and stays. Beat: heartbreak as sacrifice; duty nearly wins, and love refuses to let it.

chapters.title: The Second Singing
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. A child hums a winter song twice on a dare, and that night three villagers are found standing in the square, asleep, facing the church cellar. Beat: consequence made flesh; the village's oldest rule proven necessary at terrible cost.

chapters.title: What It Wants
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. Through borrowed mouths — first the old woman, then Aldous — the thing below negotiates: it wants a Sterling to finish the founders' work, either side of the door. Beat: revelation of the trap; her ancestry is not coincidence but summons.

chapters.title: The Rite Interrupted
chapters.summary: Aldous's POV. He shows Ulyana the founders' incomplete instructions: the binding requires two singers, one above, one below, and the founders' second singer deserted. The frost patterns on every window are the ritual's unfinished notation. Beat: dawning understanding of what completion would cost.

chapters.title: Tomas Descends
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. Refusing to let her go alone, Tomas enters the cellar with rope, lamp, and his father's iron spade, and finds the second singer's skeleton still holding a tuning fork. Beat: courage as devotion; love choosing descent over safety.

chapters.title: The Frost Writes Its Final Pattern
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The cold turns absolute; the village sleeps and cannot be woken; frost completes the sigil across every surface, pointing down. Ulyana understands the winter itself is the ritual's clock running out. Beat: apocalyptic stillness before the climax.

chapters.title: Two Voices, One Door
chapters.summary: Alternating POVs. Ulyana above, Tomas below, they sing the binding together across the threshold — her voice carrying the melody, his the countermelody from the fork's tone. The thing offers Ulyana her ancestors' memories, her family, belonging, if she stops. Beat: climax; love against duty resolved into love as duty.

chapters.title: The Price of Completion
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. The seal requires memory as mortar: everything recorded, everything sung twice. Ulyana feeds her archive — tapes, notebooks, and then her own recollections of Tomas — into the closing door. Beat: sacrificial climax; the folklorist erased by her own folklore.

chapters.title: Sealed From Both Sides
chapters.summary: Tomas's POV. The door fuses shut, this time sealed from within and without, and Tomas digs himself out into a thawing morning, remembering everything she chose to forget. Beat: grief and awe; survival as the lonelier outcome.

chapters.title: Spring, Almost
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV. She packs to leave with gaps in her mind like missing teeth, drawn inexplicably to a stranger at the inn who watches her with unbearable familiarity. She cannot place him; he cannot say goodbye twice. Beat: bittersweet resolution; memory's cost paid in tenderness.

chapters.title: A Winter for the Cellar
chapters.summary: Ulyana's POV, epilogue. On the sledge out of Vinterhollow she finds one tape she never made: her own voice singing the binding song, addressed to whoever forgets. She plays it once, weeps without knowing why, and lets the wind take it. Beat: closure; belonging found in the giving away.
